items.name: Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group Sails in the Philippine Sea for Keen Sword Drills
items.summary: The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group, as well as Japanese, Australian, Canadian and French warships, have gathered in the Philippine Sea to participate in exercise Keen Sword 27. The Theodore Roosevelt CSG steamed alongside ships from the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force Royal Australian Navy, Royal Canadian Navy and French Navy on Wednesday in the Philippine Sea, according to a Pentagon imagery release. The imagery shows flagship USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) and USS Chosin (CG-65) sailing with JMSDF helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182) and destroyers JS Kongo (DDG-173) and destroyer JS Asahi (DD-119), RAN frigate HMAS Stuart (FFH153), RCN frigate HMCS

items.name: NATO Kicks Off Neptune Strike Across European Waters
items.summary: NATO kicked off enhanced Vigilance Activity Neptune Strike 26-4 on Friday, the fourth and final iteration this year.  The enhanced Vigilance Activity will feature the U.K and Italian carrier strike groups and the Turkish Anadolu Naval Task Group will span Northern, Central and Southern Europe until Nov. 5. In total, 17 NATO nations will participate in NEST 26-4. Drills will be held from the Mediterranean to the Baltic regions, with operations extending across all three NATO Joint Operations Areas. items.name: USS Abraham Lincoln to shift home port to Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton
items.summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln is shifting its home port from San Diego to Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton, Washington, according to a recent service announcement.
items.full_text:
TheUSS Abraham Lincolnis shifting its home port from San Diego to Naval Base Kitsap-Bremerton, Washington, according to a recent service announcement.

The relocation is expected to be completed later this year and executed as a permanent change of station for the aircraft carrier’s crew and family members. The move, while long planned, had left many family members in limbo after the USS Abraham Lincoln’s routine six-monthdeploymentwas extended twice after the U.S. jointly launched Operation Epic Fury with Israel on Feb. 28.

The ship, which returned to San Diego, California, on Oct. 8, spent 322 days at sea — and 265 consecutive days without a port call.

At an August town hall meeting in San Diego, family members spoke with Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and other senior officials, expressing frustration with Navy officials over reported food shortages, concerns about self-harm and confusion over the timeline regarding theimpending move to Washington.

According to the release, the home port shift is part of the Navy’s “strategic dispersal of ships,” while noting that “Regularly scheduled depot-level maintenance maximizes the lifespan of our Navy vessels and keeps our fleets lethal, modern, and ready to defend the nation. The work conducted during the maintenance period will maximize the lifespan of Abraham Lincoln and re-establish the carrier at the highest state of material and combat readiness.”

The Navy did not provide a start date for the maintenance period. Naval Base Kitsap is the Navy’s third-largest Fleet Concentration Area and its most complex multi-mission installation, according to its website. The Lincoln will join its fellow Nimitz-class carrier, USS Ronald Reagan, in Kitsap.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced on Oct. 7 that the carrier strike group had been awarded the Presidential Unit Citation, the military’s highest unit-level valor award.

Hegseth, who visited the carrier one day prior to the ship reaching shore, announced the award to the 5,000 sailors aboard the Lincoln, citing the “historic mission” that included completing “3,693 combat flights, sinking 64 Iranian warships, launching 450 Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles and shooting down 77 one-way aerial attack drones.”

Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.
